species.name: Helicoverpa zea
notes: Corn earworm: attacks corn, cotton, soybean and tomato; a main target of Bt traits and resistance monitoring.
Its caterpillars eat corn ears, cotton bolls and tomato fruit, so it meets many different insecticide programs.
Resistance to some Bt proteins has been reported in the field, so refuges and monitoring matter.

species.name: Helicoverpa armigera
notes: Old World bollworm: a polyphagous pest of cotton, corn and legumes with widespread insecticide resistance.
Pyrethroid resistance became widespread in this species on cotton in several countries.
Resistance management relies on refuges and rotating modes of action.

species.name: Spodoptera frugiperda
notes: Fall armyworm: invasive maize pest across Africa and Asia; resistance to Bt and pyrethroids is documented.
Corn and rice strains differ in host plant, which matters when designing refuges.
Its rapid spread since 2016 has pushed smallholder maize growers toward new insecticide use.

species.name: Spodoptera exigua
notes: Beet armyworm: attacks vegetables and cotton and is often resistant to several insecticide classes.
Resistance to both spinosyns and diamides has been reported.
A nucleopolyhedrovirus is registered as a very selective biological control for it.

species.name: Ostrinia nubilalis
notes: European corn borer: a maize stem borer and a classic target of Bt corn.
Area-wide Bt corn use has suppressed its numbers, which also benefits nearby non-Bt crops.
Bt corn aimed at this borer sparked the monarch pollen debate over non-target effects.

species.name: Agrotis ipsilon
notes: Black cutworm: cuts maize and vegetable seedlings at the soil surface.
Moths migrate long distances, so infestations can appear without local overwintering.
Pyrethroid soil treatments and Bt traits are common controls.

species.name: Plutella xylostella
notes: Diamondback moth: attacks brassicas and was the first insect to evolve field resistance to Bt sprays.
It has evolved resistance to dozens of insecticide active ingredients.
The parasitoid wasps that help control it are easily killed by broad-spectrum sprays.

species.name: Trichoplusia ni
notes: Cabbage looper: a brassica and greenhouse pest; Bt sprays are a common control.
Resistance to Bt sprays has evolved in greenhouse populations.
Cell lines from this moth are widely used in labs to make baculovirus-expressed proteins.

species.name: Pieris rapae
notes: Imported cabbageworm: a brassica pest attacked by Cotesia parasitoid wasps.
Bt-based sprays are selective for caterpillars and spare most beneficial insects.
Sprays on flowering brassicas and weeds nearby can expose visiting pollinators.

species.name: Chrysodeixis includens
notes: Soybean looper: a soybean and cotton defoliator with documented insecticide resistance.
Resistance to several insecticide classes has been reported.
Bt soybean in Brazil targets this species and the velvetbean caterpillar.

species.name: Anticarsia gemmatalis
notes: Velvetbean caterpillar: a soybean defoliator in the Americas, controlled by a baculovirus in Brazil.
The Brazilian baculovirus program has treated well over a million hectares of soybean.
Baculoviruses are highly host-specific, so they spare natural enemies and pollinators.

species.name: Manduca sexta
notes: Tobacco hornworm: a tobacco and tomato pest, host of the Cotesia wasp and a model insect.
It tolerates nicotine and is a model for studying plant chemical defenses.
Hornworms covered in wasp cocoons are best left alone, because the wasps keep future hornworms down.

species.name: Pectinophora gossypiella
notes: Pink bollworm: a cotton pest suppressed in the US by Bt cotton and sterile moth releases.
Bt cotton plus sterile moth releases helped eliminate it from US cotton areas.
Field resistance to Bt cotton has been documented in India.

species.name: Cydia pomonella
notes: Codling moth: an apple and pear pest managed with mating disruption and a granulovirus.
Pheromone mating disruption reduces insecticide sprays in orchards.
The codling moth granulovirus is a registered, highly specific biopesticide.

species.name: Aspila molesta
notes: Oriental fruit moth (also Grapholita molesta): a peach and apple pest, often managed by mating disruption.
Pheromone mating disruption is widely used against it in peach orchards.
Macrocentrus wasps help keep it in check.

species.name: Phthorimaea absoluta
notes: Tomato leafminer (formerly Tuta absoluta): an invasive tomato pest that is often resistant to insecticides.
It reached Europe in 2006 and has since spread across the Mediterranean region and beyond.
Predatory mirid bugs are used against it in greenhouse tomato.

species.name: Diatraea saccharalis
notes: Sugarcane borer: a stem borer of sugarcane, maize and rice, controlled with Cotesia flavipes wasps.
Cotesia flavipes wasps are released across Brazilian sugarcane to control it.
Bt maize in the Americas targets it among other stem borers.

species.name: Chilo suppressalis
notes: Asiatic rice borer: a rice stem borer targeted by Bt rice research.
Bt rice lines active against it have been developed in China, though not widely commercialized.
Insecticide use on rice affects aquatic life in paddies, so borer control is an ecotoxicology topic.

species.name: Leptinotarsa decemlineata
notes: Colorado potato beetle: a classic case of rapid resistance to dozens of insecticides.
Resistance to DDT appeared in the 1950s, and other chemistries have followed.
Neonicotinoid seed treatments in potato mainly target it, raising questions about soil and water residues.

species.name: Diabrotica virgifera
notes: Western corn rootworm: larvae eat maize roots; it has evolved resistance to rotation, insecticides and Bt traits.
In parts of the US Midwest, beetles adapted to lay eggs in soybean, defeating corn-soybean rotation.
Bt and RNAi-based traits have been developed against its larvae.

species.name: Diabrotica undecimpunctata
notes: Spotted cucumber beetle: feeds on cucurbits, corn and beans and spreads bacterial wilt.
Adults feed on cucurbit flowers, where they overlap with foraging pollinators.
Cucurbitacins in squash attract this beetle, a rare case of a plant toxin acting as a lure.

species.name: Anthonomus grandis
notes: Boll weevil: a cotton pest whose eradication program reshaped insecticide use in the US.
Organophosphates such as malathion were heavily used in its eradication program.
Pheromone-baited traps are used to monitor it.

species.name: Cerotoma trifurcata
notes: Bean leaf beetle: a soybean and bean pest that transmits bean pod mottle virus.
Scouting thresholds are used to limit sprays against it.
Seed treatments are sometimes used against early-season beetles.

species.name: Epilachna varivestis
notes: Mexican bean beetle: a plant-feeding lady beetle relative that skeletonizes bean leaves.
The wasp Pediobius foveolatus is released against it in the eastern US.
Unlike most lady beetles, it eats plants rather than aphids.

species.name: Phyllotreta striolata
notes: Striped flea beetle: shot-holes brassica seedlings; seed treatments protect canola.
Neonicotinoid seed treatments on Canadian canola are aimed mainly at flea beetles.
Concern about neonicotinoids and bees has put seed-treated brassica crops in the spotlight.

species.name: Psylliodes chrysocephala
notes: Cabbage stem flea beetle: an oilseed rape pest in Europe with widespread pyrethroid resistance.
After the EU restricted neonicotinoid seed treatments in 2013, growers reported more damage from it.
Pyrethroid resistance mutations are common across Europe.

species.name: Brassicogethes aeneus
notes: Pollen beetle: eats oilseed rape buds and is a key reason for pyrethroid sprays near flowering.
Pyrethroid resistance is widespread, so growers rely on thresholds and other modes of action.
Spraying oilseed rape in flower can expose bees, so label rules restrict timing.

species.name: Sitona lineatus
notes: Pea leaf weevil: notches pea and bean leaves while its larvae feed on root nodules.
Root nodule damage reduces nitrogen fixation, a key service of legume crops.
Non-chemical options include trap crops and field-edge management.

species.name: Oulema melanopus
notes: Cereal leaf beetle: a small-grain pest that is successfully held down by a parasitoid wasp.
The wasp Tetrastichus julis was released in the US from the 1960s and now suppresses it.
Broad-spectrum sprays can disrupt that biocontrol wasp.

species.name: Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus
notes: Rice water weevil: a major US rice pest, and flooded rice fields mean runoff matters.
Pyrethroid sprays on rice can be very toxic to crayfish and fish in paddies.
Water holding periods after rice insecticide use protect downstream aquatic life.

species.name: Popillia japonica
notes: Japanese beetle: grubs eat turf roots and adults skeletonize leaves of many crops.
Soil neonicotinoid use on lawns can reach flowering clover and affect bees.
The milky spore bacterium is a biological control for its grubs.

species.name: Conotrachelus nenuphar
notes: Plum curculio: a weevil that scars stone and pome fruit and is mostly controlled with orchard sprays.
Sprays at petal fall target it, so timing relative to bloom matters for bees.
Entomopathogenic nematodes can control its soil-dwelling larvae.

species.name: Agriotes lineatus
notes: Lined click beetle: its wireworm larvae damage potato and cereal roots.
Wireworms live for several years in soil, which makes them hard to control.
Pheromone traps are used to monitor adults.

species.name: Sitophilus oryzae
notes: Rice weevil: a stored-grain pest that lives inside kernels; fumigants and grain protectants are used.
Phosphine fumigation is the main grain treatment, and resistance to it is increasing.
Diatomaceous earth is a low-toxicity grain protectant.

species.name: Tribolium castaneum
notes: Red flour beetle: a stored-product pest and a model insect for genetics and toxicology.
It is a standard insect for toxicology and RNAi studies thanks to its sequenced genome.
Phosphine resistance is widespread in stored-product beetles, including this one.

species.name: Aphis glycines
notes: Soybean aphid: invasive in North America since 2000; managed with scouting thresholds and foliar sprays.
Lady beetles and Orius bugs can hold it below threshold when sprays spare them.
Pyrethroid resistance has been reported in Midwestern populations.

species.name: Aphis gossypii
notes: Cotton-melon aphid: a virus vector with a huge host range and frequent insecticide resistance.
Neonicotinoid resistance has been recorded in cotton and vegetable crops.
It reproduces asexually and fast, so resistance genes spread quickly.

species.name: Myzus persicae
notes: Green peach aphid: transmits many plant viruses and is resistant to many insecticide classes.
It has resistance mechanisms to organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids and neonicotinoids.
Resistance monitoring for this aphid is routine in Europe.

species.name: Rhopalosiphum padi
notes: Bird cherry-oat aphid: a cereal pest that vectors barley yellow dwarf virus.
Seed treatments in cereals are partly aimed at its virus transmission.
Parasitoids and hoverflies are important natural enemies of it in cereals.

species.name: Rhopalosiphum maidis
notes: Corn leaf aphid: feeds in maize whorls and tassels and on sorghum and barley.
Natural enemies often keep it below economic levels in maize.
It is a vector of maize dwarf mosaic virus.

species.name: Sitobion avenae
notes: English grain aphid: a wheat and barley pest that feeds many natural enemies.
Pirimicarb is a selective aphicide used to spare natural enemies.
Pyrethroid resistance (kdr) has been found in UK populations.

species.name: Acyrthosiphon pisum
notes: Pea aphid: a legume pest and genomics model that ladybirds and parasitoids feed on.
Bacterial symbionts can protect pea aphids against parasitoid wasps.
Its genome was among the first sequenced for a hemipteran.

species.name: Bemisia tabaci
notes: Silverleaf whitefly: a species complex that vectors begomoviruses and resists many insecticides.
Resistance to neonicotinoids, pyrethroids and other classes is common worldwide.
Predators, parasitoids, soaps and oils are used where broad-spectrum sprays have failed.

species.name: Trialeurodes vaporariorum
notes: Greenhouse whitefly: a protected-crop pest controlled with Encarsia wasps and selective chemistries.
Encarsia formosa was one of the first commercial biocontrol agents, in use since the 1920s.
Broad-spectrum sprays in greenhouses can wipe out those wasps.

species.name: Diaphorina citri
notes: Asian citrus psyllid: vectors citrus greening, and heavy spraying against it also hits non-targets.
Foliar insecticide use against it is heavy in Florida citrus, with effects on natural enemies and bees.
The parasitoid wasp Tamarixia radiata is released against it.

species.name: Nilaparvata lugens
notes: Brown planthopper: a rice pest whose outbreaks have followed insecticide overuse.
Broad-spectrum sprays killed spiders and mirid predators, triggering planthopper outbreaks.
Resistance to imidacloprid is widespread in Asia.

species.name: Empoasca fabae
notes: Potato leafhopper: its saliva causes hopperburn in alfalfa, potato and beans.
Alfalfa varieties with hairy leaves reduce damage.
Spray timing around alfalfa bloom matters for bees.

species.name: Lygus lineolaris
notes: Tarnished plant bug: sucks buds and fruit of cotton, strawberry and many crops; pyrethroid resistance is reported.
It feeds on many weeds, which act as alternate hosts around fields.
Sprays against it can flare secondary pests by killing predators.

species.name: Lygus hesperus
notes: Western tarnished plant bug: a key pest of cotton and alfalfa seed in the western US.
Strip-cutting alfalfa leaves refuges that protect beneficial insects.
Flonicamid and other more selective products are used against it.

species.name: Halyomorpha halys
notes: Brown marmorated stink bug: an invasive fruit and vegetable pest whose broad-spectrum sprays disrupt IPM.
The samurai wasp, Trissolcus japonicus, is a biocontrol agent that has reached the US.
Sprays against it can flare secondary pests such as mites and scale.

species.name: Nezara viridula
notes: Southern green stink bug: a worldwide pest of soybean, cotton and vegetables.
Egg parasitoids such as Trissolcus basalis are used in biocontrol.
It feeds on many hosts, so sprays in one crop can push it into neighboring crops.

species.name: Euschistus servus
notes: Brown stink bug: feeds on cotton, corn and soybean seeds and fruit.
Pyrethroid sprays against stink bugs are linked to later outbreaks of aphids and mites.
Trap crops at field edges can concentrate it before spraying.

species.name: Megacopta cribraria
notes: Kudzu bug: invasive in the southeastern US, feeding on kudzu and soybean.
An egg parasitoid from Asia, Paratelenomus saccharalis, now attacks it in the US.
Pyrethroid sprays on soybean can suppress natural enemies.

species.name: Murgantia histrionica
notes: Harlequin bug: a brassica specialist, often hand-picked or trap-cropped in organic systems.
Collards and mustards planted as trap crops pull it away from cabbage.
Egg parasitoid wasps help limit it.

species.name: Anasa tristis
notes: Squash bug: a cucurbit pest; its fly parasitoid is also in this deck.
Squash flowers heavily, so sprays during bloom can harm pollinators such as squash bees.
Hand-picking egg masses and trapping under boards reduce the need to spray.

species.name: Leptoglossus phyllopus
notes: Eastern leaf-footed bug: feeds on fruit and seeds of tomato, citrus, cotton and sorghum.
It is a mobile bug that moves between crops and wild hosts.
Egg parasitoid wasps are among its natural enemies.

species.name: Lycorma delicatula
notes: Spotted lanternfly: an invasive planthopper that attacks grapevines and fruit trees.
Systemic insecticides applied to trees against it raise pollinator exposure concerns.
Its honeydew supports sooty mold on vines and fruit.

species.name: Frankliniella occidentalis
notes: Western flower thrips: vectors tospoviruses, hides in flowers and often resists insecticides.
Resistance to spinosyns and pyrethroids has been documented.
Predatory mites and Orius bugs are released to control it in greenhouses.

species.name: Thrips tabaci
notes: Onion thrips: an onion and cabbage pest that vectors iris yellow spot virus.
Some populations reproduce without males, which speeds the spread of resistance.
Insecticide programs in onion rotate modes of action to slow resistance.

species.name: Tetranychus urticae
notes: Two-spotted spider mite (a mite, not an insect): outbreaks often follow sprays that kill its predators.
It has evolved resistance to a very large number of acaricides.
Predatory mites only help if sprays spare them.

species.name: Drosophila suzukii
notes: Spotted wing drosophila: lays eggs in ripening soft fruit, driving frequent insecticide use.
Spinosyn and pyrethroid sprays on ripening fruit raise residue and bee-exposure questions.
Netting and sanitation can cut sprays on small fruit.

species.name: Ceratitis capitata
notes: Mediterranean fruit fly: a fruit pest managed with bait sprays and the sterile insect technique.
The sterile insect technique releases sterilized males with no insecticide on the crop.
Protein-bait sprays with spinosad use relatively little insecticide.

species.name: Bactrocera dorsalis
notes: Oriental fruit fly: an invasive fruit pest; methyl eugenol lures are used for detection and male annihilation.
Male annihilation mixes the lure with a small amount of insecticide.
It has been the target of large eradication campaigns in California and Florida.

species.name: Delia radicum
notes: Cabbage root fly: larvae damage brassica roots; seed treatments and covers are used.
Organophosphate soil insecticides once widely used against it have been restricted in many regions.
Fine insect netting is a non-chemical option.

species.name: Melanoplus differentialis
notes: Differential grasshopper: feeds on soybean, corn and alfalfa near field margins.
Grasshopper sprays on field margins can hit pollinators and ground beetles.
US western grasshopper control programs use diflubenzuron, an insect growth regulator.

species.name: Locusta migratoria
notes: Migratory locust: a swarming crop pest; barrier sprays raise non-target concerns for other arthropods.
Outbreak control uses sprays such as fipronil, and effects on non-target arthropods are monitored.
The biopesticide Metarhizium acridum is a lower-impact alternative.

species.name: Schistocerca gregaria
notes: Desert locust: plague swarms threaten food security; control uses sprays and the fungus Metarhizium.
Past swarm control with organophosphates prompted study of effects on birds and non-target insects.
Insect growth regulators and Metarhizium are used for barrier treatments.

species.name: Solenopsis invicta
notes: Red imported fire ant: invasive; it attacks crop seedlings and is treated with insecticide baits.
Baits containing insect growth regulators avoid broadcast sprays.
Phorid fly parasitoids have been released as biocontrol.

species.name: Hippodamia convergens
notes: Convergent lady beetle: an aphid predator sold for biocontrol that broad-spectrum sprays can harm.
Larvae and adults eat aphids, so contaminated prey is an exposure route.
It migrates to mountains to overwinter, and wild-collected beetles are sold.

species.name: Harmonia axyridis
notes: Multicolored Asian lady beetle: an introduced aphid predator that now outcompetes native lady beetles.
It is used as a test species in studies of pesticide and Bt-crop effects on predators.
It makes harmonine, a defensive alkaloid.

species.name: Coccinella septempunctata
notes: Seven-spot ladybird: a common aphid predator used as a non-target test species.
Larvae are more sensitive than adults to many insecticides.
Its spread in North America coincided with declines of some native lady beetles.

species.name: Adalia bipunctata
notes: Two-spot ladybird: an aphid predator used as a non-target test species in Europe.
Its short life cycle makes it practical for laboratory toxicity testing.
It eats aphids, scales and psyllids in orchards.

species.name: Coleomegilla maculata
notes: Spotted lady beetle: eats aphids, eggs and corn pollen, so it features in Bt corn non-target studies.
Pollen feeding exposes it to toxins expressed in corn pollen.
It also eats Colorado potato beetle eggs.

species.name: Chrysoperla carnea
notes: Green lacewing: larvae eat aphids; a standard non-target test species in pesticide risk assessment.
Larvae are voracious predators, while adults feed on nectar and honeydew.
Pesticide-tolerant strains have been selected for use in sprayed crops.

species.name: Chrysoperla rufilabris
notes: Common green lacewing in the southeast US; larvae eat aphids, mites and insect eggs.
Larvae are sold commercially for release in greenhouses and orchards.
Adults feed on honeydew and pollen, so flowering margins help them.

species.name: Orius insidiosus
notes: Insidious flower bug: a predator of thrips, mites and corn earworm eggs.
It is sensitive to pyrethroids and many broad-spectrum sprays.
Commercial Orius are released for thrips control in greenhouses.

species.name: Geocoris punctipes
notes: Big-eyed bug: an omnivorous predator of mites, eggs and small caterpillars in cotton and soybean.
It also feeds on plants, which exposes it to systemic insecticides.
In cotton, sprays against bollworm can reduce its numbers.

species.name: Nabis roseipennis
notes: Damsel bug: a generalist predator of aphids and caterpillars in field crops.
Foliar sprays often reduce damsel bugs, letting pests rebound.
It eats alfalfa weevil larvae, aphids and caterpillars.

species.name: Podisus maculiventris
notes: Spined soldier bug: a predatory stink bug that attacks caterpillars and beetle larvae.
It stabs prey with its beak and injects digestive enzymes.
Some insecticides that spare it are chosen precisely for that reason.

species.name: Perillus bioculatus
notes: Two-spotted stink bug: a predator of Colorado potato beetle eggs and larvae.
Resistance to insecticides in potato beetles makes predators like this one more valuable.
It is reared commercially in some countries for release.

species.name: Zelus longipes
notes: Longlegged assassin bug: a generalist ambush predator of crop margins and gardens.
Assassin bugs can be harmed when they eat sprayed prey.
Sticky secretions on the forelegs of some Zelus help hold prey.

species.name: Calosoma scrutator
notes: Fiery searcher beetle: climbs plants to hunt caterpillars, including armyworms.
Adults and larvae both eat caterpillars.
It is large and long-lived, so repeated spray exposure is a concern.

species.name: Pterostichus melanarius
notes: A common ground beetle of crop fields: eats slugs, aphids and seeds, and appears in pesticide studies.
It is a frequent subject of field and laboratory studies on pesticide effects on carabids.
It eats slugs, which are pests in cereals and oilseed rape.

species.name: Poecilus cupreus
notes: Copper ground beetle: a European field carabid often used as a non-target test species.
Carabid tests often use larvae because they live in treated soil.
It eats aphids, fly larvae and seeds in cereal fields.

species.name: Harpalus pensylvanicus
notes: Pennsylvania dingy ground beetle: eats weed seeds and insects in crop fields.
Seed-eating carabids reduce weed seed banks, a service herbicides can disrupt.
Feeding on seeds can expose it to treated seed coats.

species.name: Aleochara bilineata
notes: A rove beetle that parasitizes cabbage root fly pupae and is a standard non-target test species.
Larvae parasitize fly pupae in the soil, so soil insecticides can harm the next generation.
It appears in EU non-target arthropod testing guidance.

species.name: Cotesia congregata
notes: A parasitoid wasp whose larvae kill tobacco hornworms; the white cocoons are easy to spot.
Viruses carried by the wasp suppress the host caterpillar's immune system.
Parasitized caterpillars eat less and stop damaging the crop.

species.name: Aphidius ervi
notes: A parasitoid wasp that turns pea and grain aphids into golden mummies; very sensitive to many insecticides.
Mummies are tan, bloated aphids with a round exit hole.
Banker plants maintain these wasps in greenhouses.

species.name: Trichopoda pennipes
notes: Feather-legged fly: a tachinid parasitoid of squash bugs and stink bugs.
Females lay eggs on the bug's body, so the larva burrows in and feeds from inside.
Parasitized bugs often carry white eggs behind the head.

species.name: Toxomerus politus
notes: Maize calligrapher: a small hoverfly whose larvae eat aphids and adults feed on corn pollen.
Adults feed on corn pollen, so they are exposed to anything expressed in it.
Larvae eat corn leaf aphids and other small insects.

species.name: Allograpta obliqua
notes: Oblique streaktail: a hoverfly whose larvae eat aphids; adults pollinate.
Larvae are legless, green-yellow maggots that cluster near aphids.
Hoverfly larvae are sensitive to many insecticides and are often missing from sprayed crops.

species.name: Episyrphus balteatus
notes: Marmalade hoverfly: a migratory aphid predator whose adults also pollinate.
Hoverfly larvae can eat hundreds of aphids before they pupate.
Adults migrate across Europe in large numbers.

species.name: Forficula auricularia
notes: European earwig: eats aphids and orchard pests but can also damage soft fruit.
Earwig numbers are reduced by pyrethroid and organophosphate sprays.
As an omnivore, it is both an orchard predator and a soft-fruit pest.

species.name: Pardosa milvina
notes: A wolf spider common in crop fields and used in studies of pesticide effects on spiders.
Wolf spiders hunt on the ground and are exposed through soil and contact with sprays.
Sublethal doses of some insecticides have been reported to change their hunting and mating behavior.

species.name: Oxyopes salticus
notes: Striped lynx spider: an ambush predator on cotton and soybean foliage.
Lynx spiders hunt on plants, so foliar sprays reach them directly.
It eats bollworm eggs and larvae in cotton.

species.name: Phidippus audax
notes: Bold jumping spider: hunts crop pests including caterpillars and beetles.
Jumping spiders have excellent vision and hunt without webs.
Spiders in field crops can suffer from broad-spectrum sprays, which lowers natural pest control.

species.name: Phytoseiulus persimilis
notes: A predatory mite released against two-spotted spider mites; sensitive to many pesticides.
It specializes on spider mites, so sprays that kill it can bring the mites back.
Pesticide compatibility tables are published for commercial biocontrol users.

species.name: Neoseiulus californicus
notes: A predatory mite released against spider mites and thrips in orchards, berries and greenhouses.
Predatory mites are easily harmed by broad-spectrum sprays, so compatibility with pesticides is tested before release.
Strains tolerant of some insecticides have been selected for use in sprayed crops.

species.name: Apis mellifera
notes: Western honey bee: the standard test species for pollinator pesticide risk assessment.
Standard tests include acute oral and contact toxicity (OECD 213, 214) and chronic and larval tests.
Colony feeding studies and semi-field tunnel tests add higher tiers of risk assessment.

species.name: Bombus impatiens
notes: Common eastern bumble bee: a commercial greenhouse pollinator and a model for pesticide effects.
Colonies are bought for greenhouse tomatoes and used in laboratory exposure studies.
Neonicotinoid exposure has been shown to reduce bumble bee colony growth.

species.name: Bombus terrestris
notes: Buff-tailed bumble bee: the bumble bee most used in European pesticide tests.
A 2012 study found field-realistic imidacloprid exposure reduced queen production.
OECD guidance documents 246 and 247 cover bumble bee acute tests.

species.name: Bombus vosnesenskii
notes: Yellow-faced bumble bee: a key pollinator of West Coast crops such as berries and tomatoes.
Bumble bees in orchards and berry fields forage where sprays are common.
Surveys have found pesticide residues in pollen collected by bumble bees in agricultural areas.

species.name: Bombus bimaculatus
notes: Two-spotted bumble bee: a native eastern pollinator of fruit and vegetable crops.
Queens emerge early and visit fruit bloom.
Nests are in the ground or in cavities, so soil residues can reach them.

species.name: Osmia lignaria
notes: Blue orchard bee: a managed pollinator of almonds and tree fruit and a candidate solitary-bee test species.
Females nest in holes and use mud, so contaminated mud and pollen are both exposure routes.
Cavity-nesting bees are sensitive to systemic insecticides in pollen.

species.name: Osmia bicornis
notes: Red mason bee: the European solitary bee used in pesticide risk assessment.
Larvae eat pollen provisions, so residues in pollen matter.
EFSA bee guidance includes solitary bees such as Osmia in risk assessment.

species.name: Osmia cornifrons
notes: Japanese hornfaced bee: a managed apple pollinator and a candidate solitary-bee test species.
It has been managed for apple pollination in Japan for decades and in the US since the 1970s.
Efforts to standardize solitary bee tests include Osmia species.

species.name: Megachile rotundata
notes: Alfalfa leafcutting bee: managed for alfalfa seed and tested as a solitary-bee surrogate.
It cuts leaf pieces to build nest cells, so contact with treated foliage matters.
Residues in leaf pieces and pollen are studied as exposure routes.

species.name: Nomia melanderi
notes: Alkali bee: a ground-nesting pollinator of alfalfa seed in the western US.
It nests in dense soil beds, so soil residues are a concern.
Managed nesting beds are protected with spray timing rules on alfalfa.

species.name: Xenoglossa pruinosa
notes: Squash bee (formerly Peponapis pruinosa): a cucurbit specialist that nests in field soil, so soil residues matter.
Females emerge at dawn to visit squash flowers.
Soil-applied systemic insecticides can reach squash pollen, so exposure has been studied.

species.name: Habropoda laboriosa
notes: Southeastern blueberry bee: buzz-pollinates blueberries in early spring.
Spray timing is restricted during blueberry bloom to protect bees.
Females buzz flowers to shake loose pollen.

species.name: Agapostemon virescens
notes: Bicolored striped sweat bee: a ground-nesting native pollinator of many crops.
Ground-nesting bees may encounter soil residues.
Its metallic green color makes it easy to spot in surveys.

species.name: Melissodes bimaculatus
notes: Two-spotted long-horned bee: a native pollinator of squash, sunflower and cotton.
Males sleep clasping plant stems at dusk.
Long-horned bees are important for sunflower seed production.

species.name: Eristalis tenax
notes: Drone fly: a pollinating hoverfly whose larvae live in nutrient-rich water.
Larvae live in polluted standing water, so they tolerate organic pollution.
Adults are among the most common flower visitors in crop fields.

species.name: Danaus plexippus
notes: Monarch: the non-target butterfly of Bt corn pollen studies, and its milkweed is lost to herbicides.
A 1999 study reported effects of Bt pollen on monarch larvae, prompting field studies that found low risk.
Milkweed loss in crop fields is a leading hypothesis for monarch declines.

species.name: Daphnia magna
notes: Water flea: the standard freshwater crustacean for acute and chronic toxicity tests (OECD 202, 211).
In the acute test, immobilisation after 48 hours is the endpoint.
Reproduction over 21 days measures chronic effects.

species.name: Daphnia pulex
notes: Common water flea: a close relative used in toxicity testing and in studies of induced defenses.
It detects fish chemicals and grows protective helmets.
Its sequenced genome supports toxicogenomics.

species.name: Chironomus riparius
notes: Non-biting midge: a sediment toxicity test species (OECD 218, 219, 233).
Larvae burrow in sediment, so it tests sediment-bound pesticides.
Emergence of adults is the endpoint in OECD 218.

species.name: Gammarus fasciatus
notes: Freshwater amphipod of eastern North America, used in aquatic toxicity tests.
Scuds shred leaf litter, so harm to them ripples through stream food webs.
Amphipods are sensitive to many insecticides, including pyrethroids.

species.name: Chironomus dilutus
notes: Non-biting midge: the standard US sediment toxicity test midge.
Larvae live in sediment, so it tests sediment-bound pesticides.
Growth and survival over about 10 to 20 days are typical endpoints.

species.name: Gammarus pulex
notes: Freshwater shrimp: a sensitive indicator of insecticide and stream pollution in Europe.
Feeding rate is a behavioral endpoint in its toxicity assays.
Its decline signals insecticide contamination in streams.

species.name: Hexagenia limbata
notes: Burrowing mayfly: used in sediment toxicity tests and a sign of recovering water quality.
Nymphs burrow in soft sediment and need good oxygen.
Mass emergences in the Great Lakes region mark improved water quality.

species.name: Cloeon dipterum
notes: Pond olive mayfly: used in aquatic mesocosm and toxicity studies of pesticides.
Eggs hatch inside the female, so it is ovoviviparous.
It is common in ponds used for outdoor mesocosm pesticide studies.

species.name: Pteronarcys californica
notes: Salmonfly: a large stonefly that is sensitive to pollution and used in aquatic toxicity tests.
Nymphs need cold, well-oxygenated streams.
Its absence can signal metal or sediment pollution.

species.name: Eisenia fetida
notes: Compost worm: the standard soil test species for earthworm toxicity (OECD 207, 222).
Earthworm reproduction tests count cocoons and juveniles.
A closely related species, Eisenia andrei, is also used under the same name.

species.name: Lumbricus terrestris
notes: Common earthworm: a soil engineer used in pesticide field studies and as a bioindicator.
Its burrows improve water infiltration, which affects pesticide transport.
Field studies measure worm abundance after pesticide application.

species.name: Folsomia candida
notes: Springtail: the standard soil arthropod for reproduction tests (OECD 232).
It reproduces without mating, which simplifies testing.
Springtails are sensitive to some insecticides and fungicides.

species.name: Armadillidium vulgare
notes: Pill bug: an isopod used as a soil bioindicator for metals and pesticides.
It is a terrestrial crustacean, not an insect.
It accumulates metals in its hepatopancreas.

species.name: Drosophila melanogaster
notes: Fruit fly: a model for insecticide resistance and neurotoxicity research.
A DDT resistance gene, Cyp6g1, was first well characterized in this fly.
Dose-response assays with neurotoxins are easy to run in it.

species.name: Lumbriculus variegatus
notes: Blackworm: a standard sediment bioaccumulation test worm (OECD 315).
In bioaccumulation tests, worms are exposed to contaminated sediment for 28 days.
It reproduces by fragmenting, so cultures are easy to maintain.
